topic.title: China's Antelope Reef Base in the South China Sea

subtopics.title: Location and Geography of the South China Sea
subtopics.summary: The South China Sea is an arm of the Western Pacific Ocean that borders the South-East Asian mainland. It is bordered by seven countries and connects with the East China Sea and the Philippine Sea through two straits. Together with the East China Sea, it forms what is termed the China Sea.

Bordered by Brunei, China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam
Taiwan Strait connects it with the East China Sea
Luzon Strait connects it with the Philippine Sea
South China Sea and East China Sea together form the China Sea
Lies in a heavily trafficked maritime zone used for a large portion of global trade

subtopics.title: Importance of the South China Sea
subtopics.summary: The sea holds large estimated reserves of oil and natural gas and has rich fishing grounds. It is also a major trade corridor, with UNCTAD estimating that over a fifth of global trade passes through it. Nearly one-third of the world's shipping trade moves through this waterway each year.

subtopics.title: Antelope Reef Development and Strategic Role
subtopics.summary: China has completed the first phase of development at Antelope Reef, which lies in the disputed Paracel Islands. The project reportedly includes an artificial island of nearly 6 km and a 680-metre wharf linked to a deep-water harbour. China says the development serves civilian purposes, but the facility could also strengthen its military infrastructure and protect its submarines.

subtopics.title: Legal Disputes: Nine-Dash Line, UNCLOS and the PCA
subtopics.summary: China's claims in the South China Sea are described through the Nine-Dash Line, which began as an 11-dashed line in 1947. UNCLOS came into force in 1994 as a legal framework, but its interpretation in this sea remains fiercely disputed. In 2016 the Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled that China's claims over 90% of the sea were illegitimate, and China rejected the ruling.

subtopics.title: Island Claims and Implications for India
subtopics.summary: The Paracel Islands are claimed by China, Taiwan and Vietnam, and China has exercised de facto control since 1974. The Spratly Islands and Scarborough Shoal also have overlapping claims, and a 2012 standoff gave China de facto control over the Scarborough region. For India, regional stability matters because much of its maritime commerce passes through this sea and the Malacca Strait.

quizzes.title: Claims, Law and Disputes
quizzes.passage:
The South China Sea has been a focus of competing territorial claims for many decades. Several countries around its shores assert rights over islands, reefs and surrounding waters, and their claims often overlap. The sea is also rich in resources and fishing grounds, which gives every claimant a practical reason to hold on to the features it controls.

After the Second World War, islands that Japanese forces had used for military purposes became part of the wider question of ownership. Claims were soon drawn on maps, and China's claim is commonly described through a boundary line marked on official maps. That line continued to appear on official maps even after the Chinese Communist Party came to power, and it covers a large share of the sea.

A United Nations convention on the law of the sea sets a legal framework that tries to balance the interests of coastal states and seafaring nations. Although the countries involved have signed and ratified it, its interpretation in this sea remains fiercely disputed. In the early 2000s, ASEAN and China agreed on a declaration meant to manage and resolve disputes.

Disputes have also gone to international bodies. The Philippines brought its case to an arbitral tribunal, arguing that China's claims violated its sovereignty. The tribunal ruled against China, which rejected the ruling and said it preferred bilateral negotiations with the other parties involved. Overlapping claims continue to shape naval activity, fishing and access to resources in the region.

questions.q: Which treaty required Imperial Japan to give up territories it had conquered during World War II?
questions.explanation: The 1951 Treaty of San Francisco forced Imperial Japan to give up territories conquered during the war.

questions.q: In which year did the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) come into force?
questions.explanation: UNCLOS came into force in 1994, providing a legal framework that balances the interests of coastal and seafaring states.

questions.q: In which year did ASEAN and China sign the Declaration on the Code of Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea?
questions.explanation: ASEAN and China signed the Declaration on the Code of Conduct in 2002 in an attempt to manage and resolve disputes.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the South China Sea:
I. It is bordered by Taiwan and Brunei, among other countries.
II. The Luzon Strait connects it with the East China Sea.
III. UNCTAD estimates that over 21% of global trade passes through it.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement II is wrong because the Luzon Strait links the sea with the Philippine Sea, while the Taiwan Strait links it with the East China Sea.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about the Paracel Islands and Scarborough Shoal are correct?
I. The Paracel Islands are claimed by China, Taiwan and Vietnam.
II. The Paracel Islands are claimed by Brunei.
III. The Scarborough Shoal is claimed by the Philippines, China and Taiwan.
questions.explanation: Statements I and III are correct, while Brunei is not listed among the claimants of the Paracel Islands.

quizzes.title: Antelope Reef Facts
quizzes.passage:
Antelope Reef has moved to the centre of debate over military activity in the South China Sea. The reef lies in a group of islands where several states have competing claims, and the area is among the busiest maritime zones in the world. Shipping that carries a large share of global trade moves through these waters every year, so any change in the region draws close attention from neighbouring countries and from trading nations far away.

Reports describe construction work that has transformed the reef, with reclaimed land, a wharf and other port facilities built alongside. Such facilities are often linked to naval use, but the government that controls the site has described its work differently and has pointed to scientific research. The reef could support larger operations over time.

Security experts have discussed what such a base could mean for the wider balance of power. A secure base for large submarines would be valuable to any navy, and a well-equipped reef could also support surveillance and patrols. Neighbouring countries have reason for concern, since military facilities on disputed features could change how the sea is used and who controls its routes.

Questions for the region now include how these developments fit into a broader plan to strengthen maritime influence, and whether other states will respond with their own installations.
